subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the Eduqas spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE Eduqas Biology simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: Light intensity and the inverse square law

questions.q: Which word equation correctly represents photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water -> glucose + oxygen, using light energy. It occurs in the chloroplasts and stores light energy as chemical energy in glucose.

questions.q: Photosynthesis is described as an endothermic reaction because it:
options: Transfers (takes in) energy from the environment, i.e. light energy
questions.explain: Photosynthesis is endothermic: energy is transferred from the environment (light) to the chloroplasts and stored in glucose. Respiration, by contrast, is exothermic.

questions.q: What is the role of chlorophyll in photosynthesis?
options: It absorbs light energy needed for photosynthesis
questions.explain: Chlorophyll is the green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy, which is then used to drive the reaction converting carbon dioxide and water into glucose.

questions.q: Which leaf feature increases the surface area for absorbing light?
questions.explain: A broad, flat leaf blade (lamina) provides a large surface area to absorb light. Palisade cells packed with chloroplasts near the top surface maximise light absorption.

questions.q: Which cells contain the most chloroplasts and carry out most photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Palisade mesophyll cells near the upper surface of the leaf are packed with chloroplasts and carry out most photosynthesis, being positioned to absorb maximum light.

questions.q: Carbon dioxide enters and oxygen leaves the leaf mainly through the:
questions.explain: Gases diffuse in and out of the leaf through the stomata, tiny pores usually on the lower surface. Guard cells open and close the stomata to control gas exchange and water loss.

questions.q: What controls the opening and closing of the stomata?
questions.explain: Guard cells surround each stoma. When turgid they open the stoma (allowing gas exchange); when flaccid they close it to reduce water loss.

questions.q: A limiting factor of photosynthesis is a factor that, when in short supply:
options: Limits (slows) the rate of the reaction
questions.explain: A limiting factor is one that, when in short/inadequate supply, restricts the rate of photosynthesis. The three main ones are light intensity, carbon dioxide and temperature.

questions.q: On a bright, warm day with plenty of light and a suitable temperature, which factor is MOST likely to be limiting photosynthesis?
questions.explain: When light and temperature are plentiful, carbon dioxide concentration often becomes the limiting factor. Greenhouses may add CO2 to increase photosynthesis.

questions.q: A graph of rate of photosynthesis against light intensity levels off (plateaus). This shows that:
options: Some other factor (e.g. CO2 or temperature) has become limiting
Light is still limiting the rate
questions.explain: When the rate plateaus as light intensity increases, light is no longer limiting - another factor such as CO2 concentration or temperature is now limiting the rate.

questions.q: Why does increasing temperature above the optimum DECREASE the rate of photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes. Above the optimum temperature these enzymes denature (active site changes shape), so the rate falls sharply.

questions.lo: Light intensity and the inverse square law
questions.q: (Higher tier) The inverse square law states that light intensity is:
options: Inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the light source
questions.explain: The inverse square law: light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance (intensity proportional to 1/d^2). Doubling the distance reduces intensity to a quarter.

questions.lo: Light intensity and the inverse square law
questions.q: (Higher tier) A lamp is moved from 10 cm to 20 cm from a pondweed. By what factor does the light intensity change?
questions.explain: By the inverse square law, doubling the distance (10 to 20 cm) reduces the light intensity to 1/(2^2) = 1/4 of its original value, slowing photosynthesis.

questions.q: Glucose made in photosynthesis can be used by the plant to:
options: Provide energy in respiration and be stored as starch
questions.explain: Glucose is used for respiration (energy), converted to starch for storage, used to make cellulose (cell walls), lipids and, with nitrate, amino acids for proteins.

questions.q: In what form do plants usually STORE glucose?
questions.explain: Plants store glucose as starch, an insoluble molecule that does not affect osmosis. Starch can be broken back down to glucose when needed for respiration.

questions.q: Plants need nitrate ions from the soil mainly to make:
questions.explain: Nitrate ions supply the nitrogen needed to make amino acids, which are joined to form proteins. A lack of nitrate causes stunted growth.

questions.q: A plant with yellowing leaves may be short of magnesium ions because magnesium is needed to make:
questions.explain: Magnesium ions are needed to make chlorophyll. A shortage causes chlorosis (yellowing leaves) and reduced photosynthesis.

questions.q: When testing a leaf for starch, the leaf is boiled in ethanol before adding iodine. Why?
options: To remove chlorophyll (decolourise) so the colour change is visible
questions.explain: Boiling in ethanol removes chlorophyll so the leaf is decolourised, making the iodine colour change easy to see. Iodine turns blue-black where starch is present.

questions.q: A positive starch test with iodine solution shows:
questions.explain: Iodine solution turns blue-black in the presence of starch. This is used to show that photosynthesis has occurred (glucose stored as starch) in the illuminated parts of a leaf.

questions.q: During the day a photosynthesising plant has a NET release of oxygen because:
options: The rate of photosynthesis exceeds the rate of respiration
It does not respire in daylight
Oxygen is a waste of respiration only
questions.explain: Plants respire all the time, but in good light photosynthesis is faster than respiration, so there is a net uptake of CO2 and net release of oxygen.
